claim: Infatuation's Madrid tapas guide highlights Juana La Loca for tortilla de patata loaded with caramelized onions, Casa Revuelta (1966) for fried bacalao, and Emma Cocina near Plaza Mayor as a local-favorite alternative to tourist traps.
quote: Juana La Loca checks all the boxes of a perfect tortilla de patata—it's loaded with caramelized onions, and the egg is never overcooked.

claim: La Campana on Calle Botoneras 6 (off Plaza Mayor) is the canonical bocadillo de calamares spot, with Bar Postas and Casa Rúa (since 1940) as the other classic picks immediately adjacent to the plaza.
quote: La Campana is a Madrid institution, and is widely considered to serve the best bocadillo de calamares in the city. It's been operating for over 70 years.

claim: Casa Camacho in Malasaña, open since the 1920s, is the archetypal Madrid vermut bar — famous for the yayo (vermouth + gin + soda) and cheap tapas on tap.
quote: Casa Camacho has been open since the 1920s, serving tapas, vermouth on tap, draught beer and wine at a very affordable price... Its offerings include 'yayos', a house special that mixes soda water, vermouth and gin.

claim: La Venencia on Calle Echegaray is a 1930s sherry-only tavern with no-photos rule, while Casa Camacho anchors the Malasaña vermut hour with the yayo cocktail.
quote: La Venencia is a historic tavern located on Calle Echegaray that has retained its original 1930s ambiance. The dimly lit space exudes an old-world charm with wood casks, dusty bottles, and weathered oak barrels.

claim: La Hora del Vermut is a pre-lunch ritual between roughly 12 and 2 pm — central to Madrid weekend rhythm and revived post-Movida as a Gen-X / millennial habit.
quote: La Hora del Vermut, or the vermouth hour, is a cherished ritual amongst Spaniards in which friends, family, or neighbors come together to enjoy an aperitivo before lunch, anytime between 12-2pm.

claim: Mercado de San Miguel is the last surviving iron-frame market hall in Madrid and draws over 7 million annual visitors across 20+ tapas stands — iconic but firmly on the tourist circuit.
quote: Located in the heart of Madrid, the Mercado de San Miguel is a monument to Spanish cuisine that welcomes more than 7 million visitors each year.

claim: Locals prefer Mercado de Vallehermoso (Chamberí, 1933) for boundary-pushing stalls and Mercado de Antón Martín for its mix of traditional butchers and standout sushi over the tourist-heavy San Miguel.
quote: Antón Martín gives you a balance of old and new, with traditional butchers and world-class sushi. This 1950s market, sitting on the border of Lavapiés, is a loud, chaotic crossroads of old Madrid and new.

claim: Vallehermoso Market opened in 1933 and its ground-floor Farmers' Gallery hosts artisan, environmentally focused producers — the locals' pick for a non-touristy market lunch.
quote: The Vallehermoso municipal market opened its doors in 1933. The market contains several stalls featuring quality produce at reasonable prices... with its ground floor occupied by the Farmers' Gallery featuring artisan food businesses.

claim: Chocolatería San Ginés (24-hour, est. 1894) and Los Artesanos 1902 are the two flagship churros-and-chocolate spots, both within a one-minute walk of each other near Sol.
quote: Churros con Chocolate at Churreria y Chocolateria Los Artesanos 1902, San Ginés and in Madrid.

claim: Los Artesanos 1902 on Calle San Martín 2 claims to be Spain's oldest churrería, now in its fifth generation, with its own stone-mill chocolate factory recreating early-20th-century texture.
quote: The churrería and chocolatería is the oldest of Spain, established since 1902 and now in its 5th generation.

claim: La Bola (since 1870) is the benchmark cocido madrileño, cooked four-plus hours in individual clay pots over oak charcoal and served in the same vessel; Lhardy (1839) and Malacatín (1895) are the other two reference houses.
quote: La Bola is the most famous cocido restaurant in Madrid... having been serving the same cocido since 1870, cooked in individual clay pots over wood fire rather than industrial ranges.

claim: Malacatín (since 1895) serves cocido in three vuelcos with the famous house challenge 'el que lo termina no paga' — finish it and you don't pay; price ranges €25–€40 across the traditional houses.
quote: Malacatín has been preparing cocido madrileño since 1895, with its motto being 'the one who finishes it doesn't pay.'

claim: Casa Lucio on Cava Baja (founded 1974 by Lucio Blázquez) is the home of huevos rotos / huevos estrellados — the perfectly fried egg broken over crisp potatoes that draws presidents, celebrities and Hollywood actors.
quote: Casa Lucio was established in 1974 by Lucio Blázquez... known nationally and internationally for its huevos rotos.

claim: Taberna Antonio Sánchez (documented 1787) is Madrid's oldest tavern, with a menu built on Madrid home cooking — oxtail, cocido, gypsy pot and callos a la madrileña.
quote: La Taberna Antonio Sánchez is the oldest tavern in Madrid, known to be prior to February 1787... Its menu is devoted to traditional Spanish and Madrid home cooking, with famous dishes including oxtail, Madrid stew, gypsy pot and Madrid-style tripe.

claim: Bodega de la Ardosa in Malasaña has been open over 125 years and is celebrated for its tortilla de patatas and vermouth on tap — the textbook Malasaña vermut-and-tapa stop.
quote: Bodega de la Ardosa is a tapas bar in Malasaña that's been open for over 125 years... Its tortilla de patatas has its own reputation and the vermouth on tap remains one of the main attractions.

claim: Sala de Despiece in Chamberí is the modern, Instagram-driven tapas counter — visually inventive small plates that have become a generational counterpoint to the centenarian taverns.
quote: Sala de Despiece is a restaurant that excels at pleasing both the eye and the palate, particularly noted for its visually appealing presentation of tapas dishes.

claim: Time Out's 2025 Madrid tapas route puts La Latina's Cava Baja crawl (Casa Labra → La Casa del Abuelo → Casa Revuelta → Tempranillo) as the canonical old-school downtown sequence, with neighborhood emphasis split between Sol/La Latina/Malasaña and newer Retiro/Chamberí.
quote: An old-school downtown route includes Casa Labra → La Casa del Abuelo → Casa Revuelta → Tempranillo (wine and toast), where you'll find Cava Baja in 4 stops with cod, prawns, fried cod and a glass of red wine near Sol.
